question: Your extraction system sent 60,000 supplier contracts through the Message Batches API with a newly written extraction prompt and JSON schema. About 30% of the extractions failed schema validation, and the resubmission rounds nearly doubled the cost of the job. The prompt had never been run on real contracts before the full batch was submitted. Which gap in the process most directly caused the high resubmission costs?

options.text: The extraction prompt was never refined on a sample set of contracts before the full volume was batch-processed.
options.reason: The guide recommends refining the prompt on a sample set before batch-processing large volumes. This maximizes first-pass success and reduces iterative resubmission costs, which is exactly what was skipped here.

options.text: The contracts went out in one large batch instead of in smaller batches submitted in four-hour windows across the weekend.
options.reason: The guide calculates submission frequency from SLA constraints. Smaller batches with the same untested prompt would fail at the same rate, so frequency does not explain the resubmission costs.

options.text: The batch requests carried no custom_id fields, so the system could not match each response to its source contract.
options.reason: The guide uses custom_id to correlate request/response pairs and to identify failed documents for resubmission. It does not raise first-pass success, so it is not why 30% of the extractions failed.

options.text: The batch had an up-to-24-hour processing window with no guaranteed latency, and this lowered the accuracy of the extractions.
options.reason: The guide describes the processing window and the missing latency SLA as properties of timing. It does not link them to extraction accuracy, so they do not explain the validation failures.
